newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks shrug off govt attempt to calm fears.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks shrug off govt attempt to calm fears.

text.p: Thai stocks lost two percent on Wednesday as investors shrugged off the government's latest bid to boost public confidence while the baht strengthened.

Concerns that more finance companies might be suspended led investors to sell stocks, especially finance firms, driving the closely-watched SET index to finish at 635.32, down 13.15 points, or 2.03 percent, from Tuesday.
The index skidded as low as 624.55 in the morning session.
A run on deposits at some banks also made the market jittery.
"Many depositors at the 42 finance companies ordered suspended by the government were still confused and not certain they would get their money back," said Bumnan Liumsuwan of Asia Credit.
"As worries mounted, many depositors withdrew their money from financial institutions still in operation".
In an attempt to restore public confidence, Thai authorities on Wednesday pledged that all deposits at non-suspended finance firms and commercial banks were fully insured.

Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said healthy Thai banks and finance firms did not face a public run on deposits, but that the market was hit by rumours of instability of financial institutions on Wednesday morning.
"The public should not panic or be confused," he said.
The assurance, which came one day after the surprise news of the suspension of 42 financial firms -- more than half of the country's finance firms.
"The market is expressing a bit of disbelief in the plan which has been announced," Donaldson Hartman, vice president at Salomon Brothers, told Reuters Financial Television.
Local depositors and finance firms had already been told in the government's announcement on the suspension of 16 finance firms in June that this was the extent of the problem.
"But this was not the end of the problem," Hartman said.

On the currency front, selling pressure on the baht subsided in the domestic market on Wednesday. The baht gained some ground to 31.50/65 to the dollar in late trading, compared with 31.70/32.00 late on Tuesday.

Thanong said on Wednesday that Thailand would lift the two-tier baht system imposed in mid-May to cut baht supplies from local sources to speculators who attacked the currency then, but he gave no date.
In the offshore market, the baht rose to 30.80/31.00, helped by a set of harsh measures unveiled on Tuesday to jack up the Thai economy, now mired in its slowest growth in over a decade.
The government pledged to boost foreign reserves, balance the budget, trim inflation and cut the current account deficit.

The package, which was recommended by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), should pave the way for a rescue loan package worth up to $15 billion by the IMF and foreign nations to help Thailand overcome its economic difficulties.
The package also gained high marks from Washington and Tokyo, but one significant question remained -- when would the loan rescue package be in place.
Some traders warn the worst may not be over yet.
They noted that it would take some time before Thailand experiences a return of foreign capital to the currency, which has plunged by about 20 percent since a de facto devaluation on July 2.

"It's hard to believe that the worst is already over for the baht. We'd better be cautious. Thailand merely set its policy target and it faces more challenges to prove it can steer the economy," a Japanese bank trader in Bangkok said.
